The exit is fast (150ms). The enter fade is slower (210ms) and delayed until the exit completes, while its slide movement runs longer (400ms): 171 172 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 173 :root { 174 --duration-exit: 150ms; 175 --duration-enter: 210ms; 176 --duration-move: 400ms; 177 } 178 179 ::view-transition-old(.slide-down) { 180 animation: 181 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both fade reverse, 182 var(--duration-exit) ease-out both slide-y reverse; 183 } 184 ::view-transition-new(.slide-up) { 185 animation: 186 var(--duration-enter) ease-in var(--duration-exit) both fade, 187 var(--duration-move) ease-in both slide-y; 188 } 189 190 @keyframes fade { 191 from { 192 filter: blur(3px); 193 opacity: 0; 194 } 195 to { 196 filter: blur(0); 197 opacity: 1; 198 } 199 } 200 @keyframes slide-y { 201 from { 202 transform: translateY(10px); 203 } 204 to { 205 transform: translateY(0); 206 } 207 } 208 ``` 209 210 The asymmetry is deliberate. Old content should leave quickly so it does not compete for attention. New content should arrive more gently so the user has time to register it. The `var(--duration-exit)` delay on the enter fade means the new content waits for the old content to finish leaving before it becomes visible. 211 212 If we refresh the page, the skeleton slides down and fades out, and a moment later the real content slides up and fades in. 213 214 ### Step 3: Add directional motion for navigation 215 216 The gallery now has morphing images and animated loading states. But navigating between pages still has no directional signal. Forward and back navigations look identical. The user cannot tell from the animation whether they moved deeper into the app or returned to a previous page. 217 218 In film and animation, horizontal direction encodes spatial position. Moving left means progressing forward (like turning a page in a left-to-right language). Moving right means going back. This convention is so ingrained that violating it feels disorienting. 219 220 Use the `transitionTypes` prop on `` to tag forward navigations: 221 222 ```tsx filename="components/photo-grid.tsx" 223 224 {/* photo thumbnail */} 225 226 ``` 227 228 The same pattern works for any navigation within the app. For example, previous/next arrows on a photo detail page can use `nav-back` and `nav-forward` to animate in the corresponding direction. 229 230 For links that return the user to a previous page, use `nav-back`: 231 232 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 233 234 ← Gallery 235 236 ``` 237 238 The transition type is not automatic. You decide which links are "forward" and which are "back" based on your app's navigation hierarchy. 239 240 Then wrap page content in a `ViewTransition` that maps transition types to directional animations: 241 242 ```tsx filename="app/photo/[id]/page.tsx" 243 256 {/* page content */} 257 258 ``` 259 260 The `enter` and `exit` props accept an object keyed by transition type. When a navigation carries the `nav-forward` type, the exit animation slides old content left and the enter animation slides new content in from the right. The `default: "none"` ensures that transitions without a type (browser back/forward, `router.refresh()`, Suspense reveals) produce no directional animation. 261 262 Wrap every participating page the same way. For the gallery to slide out on forward navigation and back in on `nav-back`, its page needs the same wrapper. Put the wrapper in each `page.tsx`, not the layout. Layouts persist across navigations, so enter and exit never fire there: 263 264 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" 265 278 279 280 ``` 281 282 The CSS for directional slides: 283 284 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 285 ::view-transition-old(.nav-forward) { 286 --slide-offset: -60px; 287 animation: 288 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 289 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 290 } 291 ::view-transition-new(.nav-forward) { 292 --slide-offset: 60px; 293 animation: 294 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 295 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 296 } 297 298 ::view-transition-old(.nav-back) { 299 --slide-offset: 60px; 300 animation: 301 150ms ease-in both fade reverse, 302 400ms ease-in-out both slide reverse; 303 } 304 ::view-transition-new(.nav-back) { 305 --slide-offset: -60px; 306 animation: 307 210ms ease-out 150ms both fade, 308 400ms ease-in-out both slide; 309 } 310 311 @keyframes slide { 312 from { 313 translate: var(--slide-offset); 314 } 315 to { 316 translate: 0; 317 } 318 } 319 ``` 320 321 The 60px offset is enough to communicate direction without making the user track a fast-moving element across the screen. 322 323 #### Anchoring the header 324 325 During directional slides, the header should not move. A sliding header breaks the user's spatial anchor. They need one fixed reference point to understand that the _content_ moved, not the entire viewport. 326 327 Assign the header a `viewTransitionName` and suppress its animation in CSS: 328 329 ```tsx filename="components/header.tsx" 330
331 {/* navigation links */} 332
333 ``` 334 335 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 336 ::view-transition-group(site-header) { 337 animation: none; 338 z-index: 100; 339 } 340 ::view-transition-old(site-header) { 341 display: none; 342 } 343 ::view-transition-new(site-header) { 344 animation: none; 345 } 346 ``` 347 348 The `display: none` on the old snapshot prevents a flash where both old and new headers are briefly visible. The `z-index: 100` ensures the header renders above the sliding content. 349 350 If we navigate forward to a photo, content slides left. If we click the "← Gallery" link (tagged with `nav-back`), content slides right. The header stays fixed throughout both transitions. 351 352 Browser-initiated back navigations (the back button or swipe gestures) do not carry a transition type, so the directional slide does not play. The shared element morph from Step 1 still applies if both pages have matching `name` props. 353 354 #### Keeping the page interactive 355 356 While a transition runs, the `::view-transition` overlay captures pointer events, so clicks during the animation are lost. Let them pass through to the live page: 357 358 ```css filename="app/globals.css" 359 ::view-transition { 360 pointer-events: none; 361 } 362 ``` 363 364 This restores interactivity for unnamed content. Hit-testing still skips named participants (like the anchored header) for the transition's duration, so keep transitions short and avoid naming elements the user clicks rapidly. 365 366 #### Respecting reduced motion 367 368 Directional slides simulate physical movement across the viewport. This is the most common trigger for motion sensitivity. The tab bar and surrounding layout do not move. Done. All four patterns are in, built and verified against the rendered output.

## What I read first

`AGENTS.md` was right to warn me off my training data — this is Next 16.3.1-canary, and the bundled `node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/02-guides/view-transitions.md` is a complete guide to exactly this task. `transitionTypes` on `<Link>` landed in v16.2.0. No config flag is needed; the App Router aliases `react` to a bundled canary (19.3.0-canary) that exports `ViewTransition`, even though top-level `react` is pinned at 19.1.0.

## Changes

**`lib/view-transitions.ts`** (new) — the shared prop bundles, so the two halves of each pair can't drift:
- `navSlide` — directional enter/exit maps
- `revealFallback` / `revealContent` — the Suspense handoff
- `morphProductImage(slug)` — one function both call sites use, so the `name`s always match

**`app/ProductGrid.tsx`** — thumbnail wrapped in the morph pair; links tagged `transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}`.

**`app/product/[slug]/page.tsx`** — hero wrapped in the matching morph pair, back link tagged `nav-back`, details Suspense boundary wrapped.

**`app/page.tsx`** and the detail page — each wrapped in `navSlide` at the page level, not the layout: layouts persist across navigation, so enter/exit never fire there.

**`app/globals.css`** — morph group + blur, slide-up/slide-down reveals, directional slides, `::view-transition { pointer-events: none }` so clicks mid-animation aren't lost, and the reduced-motion block.

**`react-canary.d.ts`** (new) — `ViewTransition`'s types live in `@types/react/canary.d.ts`, which isn't loaded by default. A triple-slash reference was the right lever here; adding a `types` array to `tsconfig.json` would have suppressed automatic `@types` discovery.

## Two judgment calls worth flagging

**Reduced motion is the refined version, not the blanket one.** The guide offers `animation-duration: 0s !important` on everything but points at a css-tricks piece arguing that's too blunt. I kept the opacity crossfades and dropped only what's positional — travel, scaling, blur — so content still reads as connected but nothing moves. Since I authored every transition class, enumerating them was safer than a wildcard; `!important` on a blanket rule would have overridden the fades I wanted to keep. I also stopped the pre-existing skeleton `pulse`, since it's an indefinite loop; the grey blocks still read as loading.

**I gave `.product-image` its own `border-radius`.** A morphing element is lifted out of the page snapshot, so the card's `overflow: hidden` stops clipping it mid-flight and the corners would square off en route to the rounded hero. The rule is a no-op at rest — visually identical to what the card was already clipping.

## Verification

Typecheck and `next build` both pass. Against the running production server I confirmed the paired `vt-name="product-image-classic-sneakers"` with `vt-share="morph"` on *both* the grid thumbnail and the detail hero, and that all 8 class-scoped rules plus all 6 keyframes survive CSS minification. I also confirmed `transitionTypes` reaches `addTransitionType` in `app-router-instance.js` rather than leaking as a stray DOM attribute.

Two things I could not verify and am not claiming: no headless browser was available in this sandbox, so **I have not watched the animations actually play**. The static evidence says the wiring is correct, but the motion itself is unconfirmed — worth a look in Chromium.

One observation I left alone: the detail page has no `<main>` wrapper, so it renders full-bleed while the grid sits in a 1200px column. That's pre-existing, and it makes the morph travel further than it otherwise would. The transition is correct either way, but if the detail page is meant to match the grid's column, fixing that would tighten the morph. Say the word and I'll do it.
